subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 62-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatic mitral stenosis reports progressive dyspnea and, over the past 3 months, difficulty swallowing solid foods. A barium esophagram shows a smooth posterior indentation of the esophagus at the level of the heart.
question: Which of the following cardiac chambers is most likely enlarged in this patient?
explanation_correct: The left atrium is the most posterior part of the heart and sits directly anterior to the esophagus. In mitral stenosis, pressure and volume back up into the left atrium, causing enlargement that can compress the esophagus and produce dysphagia, visible as a posterior impression on barium swallow. This same posterior position also explains why left atrial enlargement can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve (Ortner syndrome) and why the left atrium is the chamber best imaged with transesophageal echocardiography.

explanation_incorrect.A: The right atrium forms the right heart border and is not adjacent to the esophagus; its enlargement would not produce a posterior esophageal indentation or dysphagia.
explanation_incorrect.C: The right ventricle is the most anterior chamber of the heart; an anterior structure cannot compress the esophagus, which lies behind the heart.
explanation_incorrect.D: The left ventricle forms most of the diaphragmatic surface and the left heart border, but it is not the chamber that typically enlarges in mitral stenosis nor the one lying directly on the esophagus.
explanation_incorrect.E: The right ventricular outflow tract and pulmonary trunk are anterior and superior structures; enlargement here would not indent the posteriorly located esophagus.

educationalObjective: The left atrium is the most posterior cardiac chamber, so its enlargement (eg, mitral stenosis) can compress the esophagus and cause dysphagia.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 55-year-old woman with severe mitral stenosis is evaluated for progressive dyspnea. She has also developed a noticeably hoarse voice over the past several weeks. Laryngoscopy shows paralysis of the left vocal cord without any mass lesion in the neck or chest.
question: Which of the following mechanisms best explains this patient's hoarseness?

options.text: Compression of the right recurrent laryngeal nerve by the enlarged left atrium
Compression of the phrenic nerve as it crosses the pericardium
Direct extension of mitral valve calcification into the aortic annulus
Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by the enlarged left atrium
Reflex vagal afferent activation causing bilateral vocal cord spasm

explanation_correct: This is Ortner syndrome (cardiovocal syndrome). Because the left atrium is the most posterior part of the heart, left atrial enlargement in mitral stenosis can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve, a branch of the vagus nerve that loops under the aortic arch and ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove. Compression of this nerve paralyzes the left vocal cord and causes hoarseness.

explanation_incorrect.A: The right recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the right subclavian artery on the right side of the mediastinum and is not in contact with the left atrium; Ortner syndrome specifically affects the left nerve.
explanation_incorrect.B: The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm and the pericardium; compression would cause diaphragmatic paralysis or pericardial referred pain, not vocal cord paralysis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Valve calcification extending into the aortic annulus is a feature of calcific aortic stenosis and does not injure the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hoarseness from left atrial enlargement is a mechanical compression neuropathy, not a reflex vagal afferent phenomenon, and the laryngoscopy finding is unilateral cord paralysis.

educationalObjective: Left atrial enlargement (eg, mitral stenosis) can compress the left recurrent laryngeal nerve and cause hoarseness (Ortner syndrome).

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 24-year-old unrestrained driver is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed motor vehicle collision in which his chest struck the steering wheel. He is hypotensive with distended neck veins and muffled heart sounds. Chest imaging and echocardiography confirm a myocardial injury.
question: Which of the following structures is the most likely site of cardiac injury in this patient?
explanation_correct: The right ventricle is the most anterior part of the heart, lying directly behind the sternum, and is therefore the chamber most commonly injured in blunt chest trauma (as well as in penetrating trauma to the anterior chest). In this patient, trauma to the right ventricle with pericardial bleeding produces the classic Beck triad of hypotension, distended neck veins, and muffled heart sounds from tamponade physiology.

explanation_incorrect.B: The left ventricle is a thick-walled, posterolateral chamber; it is much less commonly injured in blunt anterior chest trauma than the right ventricle.
explanation_incorrect.C: The left atrium is the most posterior chamber and is well shielded from anterior chest impacts.
explanation_incorrect.D: The right atrium sits to the right of the midline behind the sternum's right border; although anterior-ish, it is injured less often than the right ventricle, which lies directly retrosternal.
explanation_incorrect.E: The interventricular septum lies between the ventricles and is not the most commonly injured structure in blunt cardiac trauma.

educationalObjective: The right ventricle is the most anterior chamber of the heart and is the chamber most commonly injured in chest trauma.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 48-year-old man on long-term hemodialysis develops chest pain that is worse when lying flat and improved by leaning forward; the pain radiates to his left shoulder. A friction rub is heard, and echocardiography shows a moderate pericardial effusion. Pericardiocentesis is planned.
question: From which anatomic space should the needle aspirate fluid in this patient, and which nerve carries the afferent pain fibers explaining his shoulder radiation?

options.text: Space between the fibrous and parietal pericardium; vagus nerve
Space between the epicardium and the myocardium; intercostal nerves
Space between the parietal pericardium and the epicardium; phrenic nerve
Space between the fibrous pericardium and the epicardium; sympathetic trunk
Space between the myocardium and endocardium; left recurrent laryngeal nerve

explanation_correct: The pericardium has three layers (from outer to inner): fibrous pericardium, parietal pericardium, and epicardium (visceral pericardium). The pericardial space containing effusion fluid lies between the parietal pericardium and the epicardium. The pericardium is innervated by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5), which explains referred pericarditic pain to the neck, arms, or one or both shoulders (often left).

explanation_incorrect.A: There is no fluid-filled space between the fibrous and parietal pericardial layers; they are adjacent outer layers, and the vagus nerve does not supply pericardial pain fibers.
explanation_incorrect.B: The epicardium lies directly on the myocardium with no meaningful fluid space between them, and pericardial referred pain is not carried by intercostal nerves.
explanation_incorrect.D: This pairing skips the parietal layer in the wrong order and attributes the pain pathway to the sympathetic trunk rather than the phrenic nerve.
explanation_incorrect.E: The myocardium-endocardium interface is inside the chamber and contains blood, not pericardial fluid; the left recurrent laryngeal nerve relates to left atrial enlargement, not pericardial innervation.

educationalObjective: The pericardial space lies between the parietal pericardium and the epicardium (visceral pericardium), and the phrenic nerve carries referred pericarditic pain to the neck, arms, and shoulder (often left).

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: During a pathology autopsy, a heart is removed and turned to display its inferior (diaphragmatic) surface, which rests on the diaphragm. The prosector notes that two ventricles contribute to this surface in an unequal ratio.
question: Which chamber contributes the majority (approximately two-thirds) of the inferior (diaphragmatic) cardiac surface?

options.text: Left and right ventricles contribute equally

explanation_correct: The left ventricle contributes about two-thirds and the right ventricle about one-third of the inferior (diaphragmatic) surface of the heart. This is why an inferior wall myocardial infarction, caused by occlusion of the vessel supplying this surface (commonly the posterior descending artery), involves predominantly left ventricular myocardium even though the right ventricle can be affected as well.

explanation_incorrect.A: The right ventricle contributes only about one-third of the diaphragmatic surface; it dominates the anterior surface instead.
explanation_incorrect.B: The left atrium is a posterior chamber and does not form a major part of the inferior surface.
explanation_incorrect.C: The right atrium forms part of the right heart border and does not constitute two-thirds of the diaphragmatic surface.
explanation_incorrect.D: The ventricles do not contribute equally; the split is approximately two-thirds left ventricle to one-third right ventricle.

educationalObjective: The diaphragmatic (inferior) surface of the heart is formed about two-thirds by the left ventricle and one-third by the right ventricle.
